title: Chapter 2 Mastery Quiz: Functional Neuroanatomy & Nervous System Organization
description: Test your mastery of nervous system divisions, autonomic balance, meningeal coverings, ventricles, spinal tracts, and brainstem centers.

questions.question: Which two primary structures constitute the Central Nervous System (CNS)?
questions.explanation: The CNS is anatomically defined as the brain and spinal cord, protected by the skull and spinal vertebrae.

questions.question: What is the primary role of the Somatic Nervous System (SNS)?

options.text: Mediating voluntary control of skeletal muscles and conveying conscious sensory input
Controlling unconscious visceral gut motility and heart rate
Synthesizing cerebrospinal fluid in cerebral ventricles

questions.explanation: The somatic branch of the PNS controls voluntary skeletal musculature and conveys conscious sensory sensations.

questions.question: The Sympathetic Nervous System is anatomically described as having which spinal outflow?
questions.explanation: Sympathetic preganglionic neurons emerge from the thoracolumbar region of the spinal cord (T1 to L2).

questions.question: Which cranial nerve provides the predominant parasympathetic innervation to the heart, lungs, and upper gastrointestinal tract?
questions.explanation: The Vagus nerve (CN X) accounts for approximately 75% of all parasympathetic fibers in the body, innervating thoracic and abdominal viscera.

questions.question: What is the innermost, delicate vascular layer of the meninges that adheres tightly to the surface of the brain?
questions.explanation: The pia mater is the innermost, highly vascularized translucent meningeal layer that clings directly to the brain's contours.

questions.question: Where does Cerebrospinal Fluid (CSF) circulate around the external surface of the brain and spinal cord?
questions.explanation: CSF flows within the subarachnoid space between the arachnoid membrane and the pia mater.

questions.question: Which specialized vascular structure inside the ventricles produces Cerebrospinal Fluid?
questions.explanation: The choroid plexus, composed of modified ependymal cells and capillaries, filters blood plasma to produce CSF.

questions.question: Hydrocephalus is caused by:

options.text: Excessive accumulation and abnormal buildup of CSF within the ventricular system
A sudden rupture of the myelin sheath in the cerebellum

questions.explanation: Hydrocephalus occurs when CSF production exceeds reabsorption or when ventricular outflow is obstructed, elevating intracranial pressure.

questions.question: Which glial cell extension is critical for inducing and maintaining the tight junctions of the Blood-Brain Barrier?
questions.explanation: Perivascular astrocyte end-feet envelop capillary walls and secrete signaling molecules that maintain endothelial tight junctions.

questions.question: Why can lipid-soluble substances like alcohol and nicotine cross the blood-brain barrier rapidly?

options.text: They dissolve directly through the endothelial cell phospholipid bilayer
They destroy the tight junctions upon contact
They are actively transported by ependymal cells
They travel exclusively inside white blood cells

questions.explanation: Lipophilic compounds easily diffuse across the hydrophobic lipid bilayers of capillary endothelial cells without requiring transport channels.

questions.question: The cell bodies of primary sensory afferent neurons entering the spinal cord are clustered within the:
questions.explanation: Sensory pseudo-unipolar neuronal cell bodies reside in the dorsal root ganglia situated immediately outside the spinal cord.

questions.question: Motor neurons that directly innervate voluntary skeletal muscles reside in which region of spinal gray matter?
questions.explanation: Alpha and gamma motor neurons reside in the ventral horn of the spinal cord and project their axons via the ventral roots.

questions.question: What is the primary ascending spinal tract responsible for transmitting pain and temperature sensations to the brain?
questions.explanation: The spinothalamic (anterolateral) tract conveys pain and temperature sensations from peripheral nociceptors/thermoreceptors up to the thalamus.

questions.question: An anatomical section cut parallel to the forehead, separating the front of the brain from the back, is called a:
questions.explanation: Coronal sections slice vertically perpendicular to the anterior-posterior axis, resembling slices of a bread loaf.

questions.question: In the human cerebral cortex, the anatomical term 'Dorsal' refers to which direction?

options.text: Toward the top of the head
Toward the bottom of the chin
Toward the tip of the nose

questions.explanation: In the human brain above the midbrain flexure, dorsal corresponds to superior (toward the crown/top of the skull).

questions.question: Bilateral damage to which brainstem structure causes immediate cessation of breathing and fatal cardiovascular collapse?
questions.explanation: The medulla contains the autonomic pre-Bötzinger complex and vasomotor centers essential for sustaining automatic respiration and blood pressure.

questions.question: Which structure in the midbrain tectum is responsible for mediating visual orienting reflexes, such as tracking a sudden movement in peripheral vision?
questions.explanation: The superior colliculi coordinate saccadic eye movements and visual orienting reflexes; the inferior colliculi handle auditory orienting.

questions.question: The Ascending Reticular Activating System (ARAS) running through the core of the brainstem is essential for maintaining:

options.text: Conscious cortical arousal, wakefulness, and alertness
Color vision discrimination in the fovea
Fine motor finger articulation for playing piano

questions.explanation: The ARAS projects diffuse monoaminergic and cholinergic projections across the cortex to maintain consciousness; bilateral lesions cause coma.

questions.question: What is the primary neuroanatomical consequence of damage to the Cerebellum?

options.text: Ataxia: loss of coordination, unsteady gait, and intention tremors
Flaccid paralysis and total loss of voluntary muscle control
Total cortical blindness despite healthy retinas

questions.explanation: Cerebellar lesions impair movement calibration, timing, and balance without causing paralysis, presenting as cerebellar ataxia.

questions.question: A massive infarction in the ventral pons that spares the midbrain reticular formation characteristically produces:

options.text: Locked-In Syndrome (quadriplegia and anarthria with preserved vertical eye movements and consciousness)
Deep unarousable coma with loss of all pupillary reflexes
Kluver-Bucy syndrome with hyperorality and psychic blindness
Loss of all long-term autobiographical memories

questions.explanation: Locked-In Syndrome results from ventral pontine damage severing descending motor tracts while sparing consciousness and vertical eye tracking.

questions.question: The postganglionic neurotransmitter released at most sympathetic target organs (e.g., cardiac pacemaker cells) is:
questions.explanation: Most postganglionic sympathetic fibers release norepinephrine onto adrenergic receptors (exceptions include sweat glands, which use acetylcholine).

questions.question: The 'crossed-extensor reflex' that accompanies the flexor withdrawal reflex serves to:

options.text: Extend the opposite leg to maintain upright postural support and prevent falling
Instantly freeze both arms in a protective defensive posture
Send a conscious warning signal to the visual cortex before pain is perceived
Contract the abdominal wall to protect visceral organs

questions.explanation: When the stimulated limb withdraws, contralateral spinal circuits extend the opposite limb to maintain balance and support body weight.
